claim: The mammalian order Eulipotyphla comprises moles, shrews, hedgehogs, and solenodons.
source: The speciose mammalian order Eulipotyphla (moles, shrews, hedgehogs, solenodons) combines an unusual diversity of semi-aquatic, semi-fossorial, and fossorial forms that arose from terrestrial forbearers.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a definition of the order Eulipotyphla.

claim: Eulipotyphla exhibits an unusual diversity of semi-aquatic, semi-fossorial, and fossorial forms.
source: The speciose mammalian order Eulipotyphla (moles, shrews, hedgehogs, solenodons) combines an unusual diversity of semi-aquatic, semi-fossorial, and fossorial forms that arose from terrestrial forbearers.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract describing the ecological diversity of the order.

claim: Eulipotyphlan semi-aquatic, semi-fossorial, and fossorial forms arose from terrestrial forbearers.
source: The speciose mammalian order Eulipotyphla (moles, shrews, hedgehogs, solenodons) combines an unusual diversity of semi-aquatic, semi-fossorial, and fossorial forms that arose from terrestrial forbearers.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an evolutionary pattern.

claim: The net surface charge of myoglobin (ZMb) can be readily determined from its primary structure.
source: The net surface charge of the oxygen-storing muscle protein myoglobin (ZMb), which can be readily determined from its primary structure, provides an objective target to address this question due to mechanistic linkages with myoglobin concentration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a methodological capability.

claim: ZMb has mechanistic linkages with myoglobin concentration.
source: The net surface charge of the oxygen-storing muscle protein myoglobin (ZMb), which can be readily determined from its primary structure, provides an objective target to address this question due to mechanistic linkages with myoglobin concentration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation to Mirceta et al., 2013 in the introduction.

claim: The study generated a comprehensive 71 species molecular phylogeny that resolves previously intractable intra-family relationships.
source: Here, we generate a comprehensive 71 species molecular phylogeny that resolves previously intractable intra-family relationships and then ancestrally reconstruct ZMb evolution to identify ancient lifestyle transitions based on protein sequence alone.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary result of the study.

claim: Fossorial habits evolved twice in talpid moles.
source: Our phylogenetically informed analyses confidently resolve fossorial habits having evolved twice in talpid moles and reveal five independent secondary aquatic transitions in the order housing the world's smallest endothermic divers.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding in the abstract and supported by phylogenetic and ZMb analyses throughout the manuscript.

claim: There are five independent secondary aquatic transitions in Eulipotyphla.
source: Our phylogenetically informed analyses confidently resolve fossorial habits having evolved twice in talpid moles and reveal five independent secondary aquatic transitions in the order housing the world's smallest endothermic divers.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding in the abstract and supported by phylogenetic and ZMb reconstruction analyses.

claim: Eulipotyphla houses the world's smallest endothermic divers.
source: Our phylogenetically informed analyses confidently resolve fossorial habits having evolved twice in talpid moles and reveal five independent secondary aquatic transitions in the order housing the world's smallest endothermic divers.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and elaborated in the introduction.

claim: The order Eulipotyphla consists of 527 recognized species.
source: The eulipotyphlan clade consists of 527 recognized species of small insectivorous mammals distributed among four extant families (Burgin et al., 2018): Erinaceidae (hedgehogs, gymnures, and moonrats), Soricidae (shrews), Talpidae (moles, shrew moles, shrew-like moles, and desmans), and Solenodontidae (solenodons).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Burgin et al., 2018.

claim: Eulipotyphla comprises four extant families: Erinaceidae, Soricidae, Talpidae, and Solenodontidae.
source: The eulipotyphlan clade consists of 527 recognized species of small insectivorous mammals distributed among four extant families (Burgin et al., 2018): Erinaceidae (hedgehogs, gymnures, and moonrats), Soricidae (shrews), Talpidae (moles, shrew moles, shrew-like moles, and desmans), and Solenodontidae (solenodons).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with citation.

claim: Nesophontidae (Caribbean 'island-shrews') became extinct in the past 500 years following the arrival of Europeans in the West Indies.
source: A fifth family (Nesophontidae, Caribbean 'island-shrews') only became extinct in the past 500 years following the arrival of Europeans in the West Indies (MacPhee et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to MacPhee et al., 1999.

claim: Fossil evidence supports terrestrial habits as ancestral for Eulipotyphla.
source: Fossil evidence supports terrestrial habits as ancestral for Eulipotyphla, with shrew-like moles, erinaceids, and the majority of shrews retaining morphological characteristics (e.g. slender legs and a long, pointed mouse-like snout; Figure 1) effective for hunting and avoiding predation on land (Churchfield, 1990; Nowak, 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Churchfield, 1990 and Nowak, 1999.

claim: Fossorial moles have evolved powerful forelimbs held out to the sides of their tube-shaped bodies.
source: By contrast, fossorial moles have evolved powerful forelimbs that are held out to the sides of their tube-shaped bodies and have large, spade-like hands facing posteriorly and oriented vertically allowing them to be effective burrowers (Gorman and Stone, 1990).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Gorman and Stone, 1990.

claim: Water shrews represent the world's smallest endothermic divers.
source: The secondary aquatic transitions of water shrews—which represent the world's smallest endothermic divers—are especially remarkable, given they have the lowest on-board oxygen stores, the highest mass-specific oxygen requirements, and most unfavorable surface area to volume ratios for body heat retention among all mammalian breath-hold divers (Calder, 1969; Gusztak, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Calder, 1969 and Gusztak, 2008.

claim: Water shrews have the lowest on-board oxygen stores among all mammalian breath-hold divers.
source: The secondary aquatic transitions of water shrews—which represent the world's smallest endothermic divers—are especially remarkable, given they have the lowest on-board oxygen stores, the highest mass-specific oxygen requirements, and most unfavorable surface area to volume ratios for body heat retention among all mammalian breath-hold divers (Calder, 1969; Gusztak, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Water shrews have the highest mass-specific oxygen requirements among all mammalian breath-hold divers.
source: The secondary aquatic transitions of water shrews—which represent the world's smallest endothermic divers—are especially remarkable, given they have the lowest on-board oxygen stores, the highest mass-specific oxygen requirements, and most unfavorable surface area to volume ratios for body heat retention among all mammalian breath-hold divers (Calder, 1969; Gusztak, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Water shrews have the most unfavorable surface area to volume ratios for body heat retention among all mammalian breath-hold divers.
source: The secondary aquatic transitions of water shrews—which represent the world's smallest endothermic divers—are especially remarkable, given they have the lowest on-board oxygen stores, the highest mass-specific oxygen requirements, and most unfavorable surface area to volume ratios for body heat retention among all mammalian breath-hold divers (Calder, 1969; Gusztak, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Maximum active submergence times of birds and mammals are strongly correlated to muscle myoglobin concentrations.
source: Indeed, the O2 storage function of myoglobin has long been known to contribute integrally to the mammalian dive response, with maximum active submergence times of birds and mammals being strongly correlated to muscle myoglobin concentrations (Noren and Williams, 2000; Lestyk et al., 2009; Ponganis et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Noren and Williams, 2000; Lestyk et al., 2009; Ponganis et al., 2011.

claim: Maximal muscle myoglobin concentration is mechanistically linked to myoglobin net surface charge (ZMb) in mammals via adaptive changes in primary structure.
source: Mirceta et al., 2013 extended this work to reveal that maximal muscle myoglobin concentration was mechanistically linked to myoglobin net surface charge (ZMb) in mammals via adaptive changes in primary structure, with convergent increases in ZMb found in members of all eight lineages with an extended aquatic/semi-aquatic evolutionary history.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Mirceta et al., 2013.

claim: Convergent increases in ZMb are found in members of all eight lineages with an extended aquatic/semi-aquatic evolutionary history.
source: Mirceta et al., 2013 extended this work to reveal that maximal muscle myoglobin concentration was mechanistically linked to myoglobin net surface charge (ZMb) in mammals via adaptive changes in primary structure, with convergent increases in ZMb found in members of all eight lineages with an extended aquatic/semi-aquatic evolutionary history.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Mirceta et al., 2013.

claim: An increase in ZMb may reduce the aggregation of newly synthesised, unfolded myoglobin chains (apomyoglobin).
source: An increase in ZMb may also reduce the aggregation of newly synthesised, unfolded myoglobin chains (apomyoglobin) thereby permitting efficient heme uptake and apomyoglobin folding to out compete precipitation at the high rates of translation needed to increase the cytoplasmic concentration of myoglobin while also limiting hydrophobic interactions of partially folded proteins (Samuel et al., 2015; Isogai et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Samuel et al., 2015 and Isogai et al., 2018.

claim: ZMb and maximal myoglobin concentrations are only slightly elevated within mammals that live at high elevations or have fossorial lifestyles.
source: Importantly, the finding that ZMb and maximal myoglobin concentrations are only slightly elevated within mammals that live at high elevations or have fossorial lifestyles (McIntyre et al., 2002; Mirceta et al., 2013) suggests that myoglobin primary structure may be useful to discern past semi-aquatic versus high-altitude/fossorial evolutionary histories within eulipotyphlan mammals.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to McIntyre et al., 2002 and Mirceta et al., 2013.

claim: Convergent elevations in ZMb occurred in both the American water shrew (Sorex palustris) and the star-nosed mole.
source: Support for the above contention is provided by the molecular modelling and phylogenetic reconstruction of ZMb in six eulipotyphlan species (Mirceta et al., 2013), which revealed convergent elevations in ZMb in both semi-aquatic taxa included in the dataset—the American water shrew (Sorex palustris) and the star-nosed mole.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Mirceta et al., 2013.

claim: The study used a capture hybridisation approach to target coding sequences of myoglobin together with 25 tree-of-life genes from 61 eulipotyphlan DNA libraries.
source: To overcome these shortcomings, we used a capture hybridisation approach to target coding sequences of myoglobin together with 25 tree-of-life genes from 61 eulipotyphlan DNA libraries (44 moles, 11 shrews, five hedgehogs, and one solenodon) that included representatives from all seven recognized semi-aquatic genera within this order.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a methodological approach.

claim: The study included representatives from all seven recognized semi-aquatic genera within Eulipotyphla.
source: To overcome these shortcomings, we used a capture hybridisation approach to target coding sequences of myoglobin together with 25 tree-of-life genes from 61 eulipotyphlan DNA libraries (44 moles, 11 shrews, five hedgehogs, and one solenodon) that included representatives from all seven recognized semi-aquatic genera within this order.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the study design.

claim: Twenty-three of the 25 targeted loci were efficiently captured, with usable sequence obtained from 51 to 61 libraries per locus.
source: Twenty-three of these loci were efficiently captured, with usable sequence obtained from 51 to 61 libraries per locus, equivalent to a ~95% (1330/1403) success rate (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the success of the capture hybridisation approach.

claim: The capture hybridisation approach achieved a ~95% (1330/1403) success rate.
source: Twenty-three of these loci were efficiently captured, with usable sequence obtained from 51 to 61 libraries per locus, equivalent to a ~95% (1330/1403) success rate (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific numerical data.

claim: The IRBP gene appears to be inactivated in the common ancestor of the subfamily Talpinae.
source: Notably, the putative 234 bp IRBP fragment recovered from True's shrew mole (Dymecodon pilirostris) contained gaps and premature stop codons, suggesting this gene was inactivated in the common ancestor of the subfamily Talpinae.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on sequence data showing premature stop codons.

claim: The Chinese mole shrew (Anourosorex squamipes) IRBP sequence contained premature stop codons and was presumed to be non-functional.
source: Similarly, the Chinese mole shrew (Anourosorex squamipes) IRBP sequence contained premature stop codons and was presumed to be non-functional.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on sequence data.

claim: The final alignment consisted of 39,414 bp.
source: After incorporating orthologous tree-of-life sequence data from ten additional eulipotyphlan specimens and five outgroup species downloaded from GenBank (see Materials and methods for details), our 76 specimen dataset (71 eulipotyphlans) resulted in a final alignment of 39,414 bp (Supplementary file 1b; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the final dataset.

claim: The phylogenetic analyses resulted in highly congruent topologies across different methods.
source: These analyses resulted in highly congruent topologies (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplements 2–4), with family level relationships corresponding to those obtained in recent eulipotyphlan (Brace et al., 2016; Springer et al., 2018) and mammal wide studies (Meredith et al., 2011; Esselstyn et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section comparing different phylogenetic methods.

claim: Neomys and Chimarrogale + Nectogale are not sister taxa.
source: Principal among these is the non-sister relationship of the Nectogalini water shrew clades Neomys and Chimarrogale + Nectogale, as the latter were strongly supported as sister to terrestrial Episoriculus by RAxML (bootstrap support [ML-BS]=97; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), BEAST (posterior probability [PP]=1.0; Figure 2), ASTRAL-III (coalescent bootstrap support based on gene-wise resampling [C-BS]=76; Figure 2—figure supplement 3), and *BEAST (posterior probability [C-PP]=0.99; Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with strong statistical support from multiple phylogenetic methods.

claim: Desmans are placed sister to a clade containing shrew moles, star-nosed moles, and Eurasian fossorial moles.
source: Specifically, desmans are placed sister to a clade containing shrew moles, star-nosed moles, and Eurasian fossorial moles (BS = 100, PP = 1.0, C-BS = 87, C-PP = 0.97), with Condylurini and Talpini recovered as sister lineages (BS = 72, PP = 1.0, C-BS = 52, C-PP = 0.93).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with strong statistical support.

claim: North American fossorial Scalopini moles are sister to all other Talpinae moles.
source: North American fossorial Scalopini moles are also supported as sister to all other Talpinae moles with high support scores (BS = 97, PP = 1.0, C-BS = 87, C-PP = 0.97).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with strong statistical support.

claim: A sister group relationship of fully fossorial Scalopini and Talpini moles was statistically rejected by the Shimodaira–Hasegawa (SH) test.
source: Accordingly, a sister group relationship of fully fossorial Scalopini and Talpini moles was statistically rejected by the Shimodaira–Hasegawa (SH) test (p<0.01, Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results.

claim: Complete myoglobin coding sequences (465 base pairs including initiation and stop codons) were obtained for 55 eulipotyphlan species.
source: Complete myoglobin coding sequences (465 base pairs including initiation and stop codons) were obtained for 55 eulipotyphlan species (38 moles, 14 shrews, 2 erinacids, and 1 solenodon) using capture-hybridisation, transcriptome sequencing, genome mining, and PCR approaches.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the myoglobin sequence data.

claim: No evidence for myoglobin gene paralogues was found in any of the species examined.
source: Consistent with previous surveys that indicate that myoglobin occurs as a single-copy, orthologous gene in the genomes of mammals and other jawed vertebrates (Schwarze et al., 2014), with rare, lineage-specific gene duplications being restricted to certain aquatic lineages such as some Cyprininae (carp and goldfish; Helbo et al., 2012) and Dipnoi (lungfishes; Lüdemann et al., 2020), we found no evidence for gene paralogues in any of the species examined, with conceptual translations additionally revealing the expected 153 amino-acid peptides in most cases.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to previous studies.

claim: The translated myoglobin proteins of the Chinese mole shrew, both members of the genus Scaptonyx, and the two desman genera are only 152 amino acids in length.
source: However, the translated myoglobin proteins of the Chinese mole shrew, both members of the genus Scaptonyx, and the two desman genera are only 152 amino acids in length.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on sequence data.

claim: The shorter myoglobin sequences result from 3 bp deletions in exon three that corresponded to residue position 121.
source: In every case, the shorter myoglobin sequences are the result of 3 bp deletions in exon three that corresponded to residue position 121 (Supplementary file 1d) and shorten the loop between helices G and H from 6 to 5 residues.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the molecular basis of the length difference.

claim: All charge-changing substitutions were located at the solvent-exposed surface of the protein.
source: This analysis confirmed that all charge-changing substitutions were located at the solvent-exposed surface of the protein (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on homology modelling.

claim: Deletion of position 121 in the loop between helices G and H in the myoglobin of the Russian desman has minimal effect on the tertiary structure of the protein.
source: These comparisons further suggested that deletion of position 121 in the loop between helices G and H in the myoglobin of the Russian desman has minimal effect on the tertiary structure of the protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural modelling shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The modelled ZMb values of extant semi-aquatic taxa (2.07 to 3.07) were substantially higher than those of terrestrial Eulipotyphla (−0.46 to 0.63).
source: Without exception, the modelled ZMb values of extant semi-aquatic taxa (2.07 to 3.07) were substantially higher than those of terrestrial Eulipotyphla (−0.46 to 0.63), with fossorial species generally exhibiting intermediate ZMb values (typically 1.07; Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Fossorial species generally exhibit intermediate ZMb values (typically 1.07).
source: Without exception, the modelled ZMb values of extant semi-aquatic taxa (2.07 to 3.07) were substantially higher than those of terrestrial Eulipotyphla (−0.46 to 0.63), with fossorial species generally exhibiting intermediate ZMb values (typically 1.07; Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There is a close correspondence between modelled ZMb and electrophoretic mobility of myoglobin.
source: To assess the reliability of our ZMb determinations, we measured the electrophoretic mobility of the myoglobin band of muscle extracts from two semi-aquatic, two strictly fossorial, and one terrestrial eulipotyphlan species (Figure 4B). The close correspondence between the two variables validates ZMb as a molecular marker for inferring present and past semi-aquatic habits in Eulipotyphla.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B with statistical analysis.

claim: Phylogenetic Generalised Least Squares analysis revealed a highly significant positive correlation (R2 = 0.897, p<0.005) between ZMb and electrophoretic mobility.
source: Phylogenetic Generalised Least Squares analysis in panel (B) revealed a highly significant positive correlation (R2 = 0.897, p<0.005) between the two parameters (solid line, y = 0.1488 x+0.3075).
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 4 caption with specific statistical values.

claim: The most recent common ancestor of Eulipotyphla displayed a ZMb of 0.18.
source: Ancestral ZMb estimates arising from the best fitting amino-acid based reconstruction model indicated that the most recent common ancestor of Eulipotyphla displayed a ZMb of 0.18.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on ancestral sequence reconstruction.

claim: The ZMb of the American water shrew (Sorex palustris) branch increased from −0.46 to 2.48.
source: Specifically, the ZMb of the American water shrew (Sorex palustris) branch increased from −0.46 to 2.48 and was characterised by three integral (+1) charge increasing residue replacements (Asp122→Asn122, Ser132→Lys132, and Glu136→Gln136; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on ancestral reconstruction and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The stem branch of Nectogalini evolved a single charge increasing substitution (Glu27→Ala27) and had a ZMb of 1.07.
source: The other three genera of water shrews reside in the tribe Nectogalini, the stem branch of which evolved a single charge increasing substitution (Glu27→Ala27) and thus had a ZMb of 1.07 (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The European water shrew branch (Neomys fodiens) acquired two charge increasing substitutions (Asn12→Lys12, Asp53→Ala53) resulting in ZMb = 3.07.
source: The European water shrew branch (Neomys fodiens) subsequently acquired two charge increasing substitutions (Asn12→Lys12, Asp53→Ala53; ZMb = 3.07; Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), while the common ancestor of Nectogale + Chimarrogale evolved a separate charge increasing replacement (Asp44→Ser44; ZMb = 2.07; Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: ZMb increased from an ancestral value of 0.07 to 1.07 (Ser132→Lys132) in the stem Talpinae branch.
source: Within the Talpidae, ZMb exhibited an increase from an ancestral value of 0.07 to 1.07 (Ser132→Lys132) in the stem Talpinae branch (Figure 5), with the probabilities of the identities of reconstructed amino acids at this node under the given tree and substitution model being 1.00 for all 153 sites (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The star-nosed mole branch acquired two charge increasing substitutions (Asp53→Gly53, Gln128→Lys128) and one charge decreasing substitution (Gly129→Glu129).
source: For the star-nosed mole branch this entailed two charge increasing substitutions (Asp53→Gly53, Gln128→Lys128) and one charge decreasing substitution (Gly129→Glu129; Figure 3—figure supplement 2D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in figures.

claim: The ancestral branch of the desmans acquired two charge increasing replacements (Gln26→Arg26, Asp44→Ala44) together with one charge decreasing (Asn35→Asp35) replacement.
source: The ancestral branch of the desmans also acquired two charge increasing replacements (Gln26→Arg26, Asp44→Ala44) together with one charge decreasing (Asn35→Asp35) replacement, with ZMb further being elevated in the Russian desman branch via the acquisition of an additional charge increasing substitution (Gln113→Lys113; ZMb = 3.07; Figures 3 and 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: The Russian desman has a ZMb of 3.07.
source: The ancestral branch of the desmans also acquired two charge increasing replacements (Gln26→Arg26, Asp44→Ala44) together with one charge decreasing (Asn35→Asp35) replacement, with ZMb further being elevated in the Russian desman branch via the acquisition of an additional charge increasing substitution (Gln113→Lys113; ZMb = 3.07; Figures 3 and 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in figures.

claim: The same residue positions are occasionally recruited in the charge altering replacements of semi-aquatic taxa, but the derived residues are different in all cases.
source: Notably, while the same residue positions are occasionally recruited in the charge altering replacements of semi-aquatic taxa, the derived residues are different in all cases (Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on comparison of substitutions across lineages.

claim: ThreshBayes analysis revealed a strong correlation between ZMb and aquatic adaptation (correlation coefficient r = 0.78, 95% highest posterior density [HPD]=0.48–0.93).
source: This analysis revealed a strong correlation between ZMb and aquatic adaptation (correlation coefficient r = 0.78, 95% highest posterior density [HPD]=0.48–0.93; Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific statistical values and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: ThreshBayes analyses did not support a correlation between ZMb and adaptations for digging when terrestrial and semi-aquatic eulipotyphlan species were included.
source: Conversely, threshBayes analyses did not support a correlation between ZMb and adaptations for digging, or between ZMb and a fully fossorial habit, when terrestrial and semi-aquatic eulipotyphlan species were included (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B,C.

claim: ZMb comparisons between semi-aquatic and terrestrial, and between semi-aquatic and fossorial habits were both significant.
source: Importantly, ZMb comparisons between semi-aquatic and terrestrial, and between semi-aquatic and fossorial habits (Figure 5—figure supplement 3F,G) were both significant.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3F,G.

claim: The phylogenetic estimates provide compelling evidence that the extreme anatomical specialisations for subterranean life evolved convergently in Talpini and Scalopini tribes.
source: Results of the present study thus provide compelling evidence that the extreme anatomical specialisations for subterranean life evolved convergently in these two tribes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the phylogenetic results.

claim: Ancestral sequence reconstruction of myoglobin primary structure and ZMb modelling outperform discrete, two character-state lifestyle reconstructions based on maximum parsimony and threshold approaches.
source: Here, we show that ancestral sequence reconstruction of myoglobin primary structure and ZMb modelling, with their well established mechanistic and biophysical underpinnings, outperform discrete, two character-state lifestyle reconstructions based on maximum parsimony and threshold approaches.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section comparing different reconstruction methods.

claim: The strong positive correlation between ZMb and semi-aquatic specialisation indicates that ZMb is a powerful marker to identify secondary aquatic transitions in even the world's smallest mammalian divers.
source: For example, despite being less specialised for aquatic life than marine mammals, the strong positive correlation between ZMb and semi-aquatic specialisation indicates that ZMb is a powerful marker to identify secondary aquatic transitions in even the world's smallest mammalian divers.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the correlation analysis results.

claim: ZMb is highly conserved in fossorial Scalopini and Talpini, with 23 of 25 species exhibiting a value of 1.07.
source: Although a strong correlation was not recovered between ZMb and strictly fossorial habitation, ZMb is highly conserved in fossorial Scalopini and Talpini, with 23 of 25 species exhibiting a value of 1.07.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the ZMb data.

claim: The results do not support the 'aquatic mole' hypothesis which posits that a semi-aquatic stage predated the invasion of fossorial habits in talpid moles.
source: Because ZMb of the most recent common ancestor of Talpinae was confidently estimated to be below this value (Figure 5), our results do not support the 'aquatic mole' hypothesis which posits that a semi-aquatic stage predated the invasion of fossorial habits in talpid moles (Campbell, 1939; Whidden, 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on ancestral ZMb reconstruction shown in Figure 5.

claim: The findings are consistent with the interpretation that fossorial forms evolved directly from terrestrial/semi-fossorial ancestors, without passing through a semi-aquatic phase.
source: This conclusion is supported by the results of our lifestyle reconstructions, which uniformly revealed that stem Talpinae had a low probability of semi-aquatic habits. These findings are instead consistent with the interpretation that fossorial forms evolved directly from terrestrial/semi-fossorial ancestors, without passing through a semi-aquatic phase (Reed, 1951; Hickman, 1984; Grand et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on ancestral reconstruction results and cited literature.

claim: The ZMb charge increase (to 2.07) in the stem desman branch is consistent with the semi-aquatic lifestyle of this clade being secondary to a semi-fossorial phase.
source: The ZMb charge increase (to 2.07) in the stem desman branch, paired with a lack of pronounced forelimb specialisations for digging (He et al., 2017) and a basal placement among non-scalopine Talpinae (Figure 2), also chimes with Reed, 1951 suggestion that the semi-aquatic lifestyle of this clade was secondary to a semi-fossorial phase.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section integrating ZMb data with morphological and phylogenetic evidence.

claim: The charge elevation to 1.07 in stem Nectogalini shrews temporally corresponds to the early Miocene fossil Asoriculus.
source: The charge elevation to 1.07 in stem Nectogalini shrews is enticing, as it temporally corresponds to the early Miocene fossil Asoriculus, which was theorised to have inhabited wet environments though was unlikely to have been an efficient semi-aquatic predator (Rofes and Cuenca-Bescos, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section connecting ZMb evolution with fossil evidence.

claim: The results provide strong evidence that the exploitation of semi-aquatic habits by extant shrews and talpids occurred at least five times.
source: Our results provide strong evidence that the exploitation of semi-aquatic habits by extant shrews and talpids occurred at least five times, and was accompanied by convergently evolved charge-increasing substitutions at different surface sites on the myoglobin protein in each case (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a main conclusion supported by multiple figures.

claim: Semi-aquatic habits were accompanied by convergently evolved charge-increasing substitutions at different surface sites on the myoglobin protein in each case.
source: Our results provide strong evidence that the exploitation of semi-aquatic habits by extant shrews and talpids occurred at least five times, and was accompanied by convergently evolved charge-increasing substitutions at different surface sites on the myoglobin protein in each case (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in multiple figures.

claim: The highest ZMb values were found for Russian desmans (3.07) and European water shrews (3.07).
source: It is notable that the highest ZMb values were found for Russian desmans (3.07) and European water shrews (3.07), consistent with the exceptional diving abilities of these species (Vogel et al., 2007; Ivlev et al., 2010), and it is predicted that these two species will also possess the highest muscle myoglobin concentrations among Eulipotyphla.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to diving ability studies.

claim: It is predicted that Russian desmans and European water shrews will possess the highest muscle myoglobin concentrations among Eulipotyphla.

claim: The phylogenomic analysis of myoglobin loci from tissue samples offers a useful tool to infer past semi-aquatic transitions based on myoglobin primary structure alone.
source: As such, the phylogenomic analysis of myoglobin loci from tissue samples is not only able to provide insights into the lifestyles of rare and recently extinct mammalian species (e.g. museum specimens and subfossil material from the obscure Caribbean nesophontids), but also offers a useful tool to infer past semi-aquatic transitions based on myoglobin primary structure alone.
